title: Floor and Ceil in a Sorted Array
directAnswer: In a sorted array, the floor of x is the largest element ≤ x and the ceil is the smallest element ≥ x. A linear scan is O(n); binary search makes both O(log n). Floor: move right whenever arr[mid] ≤ x (recording mid as a candidate), else move left. Ceil is the mirror: move left whenever arr[mid] ≥ x (recording the candidate), else move right. If no element qualifies, return a sentinel like −1.

remember.pattern: Binary search for a boundary, keeping the last valid candidate
remember.formula:
FLOOR (largest <= x):
  ans = -1
  while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2
    if arr[mid] <= x: ans = arr[mid]; lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1

CEIL (smallest >= x):
  ans = -1
  while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2
    if arr[mid] >= x: ans = arr[mid]; hi = mid - 1
    else: lo = mid + 1
rules: Floor and ceil are **mirror images** — same loop, opposite comparison and opposite half to keep.
Record the candidate the moment it qualifies, then keep searching the side that might do **better** (smaller gap to x).
Use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to avoid integer overflow on `lo + hi`.
If `x` is present, both floor and ceil equal `x` — the equality in `<=`/`>=` handles that for free.
When nothing qualifies (x below the min for floor, or above the max for ceil), return a sentinel (−1) — don't read out of bounds.
whenToUse: Sorted array (or monotone predicate) and you need the nearest element on one side of x
Building blocks for insert-position, range counts, and 'closest element' problems
Snapping a query to a discrete grid of allowed values
antiSignals: Array is unsorted → sort first (O(n log n)) or scan; binary search needs order
You need an exact match only → standard binary search returning the index
Data changes a lot between queries → a balanced BST / ordered set gives O(log n) with updates
Tiny array, one query → a linear scan is simpler and fast enough
remember.takeaway: Floor and ceil are the canonical 'binary search for a boundary' pattern: instead of returning on an exact hit, you stash the best candidate and keep narrowing toward x from the correct side. Master this and lower_bound/upper_bound stop being mysterious.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can adapt plain binary search from 'find an exact match' to 'find the closest element on a given side', tracking a candidate instead of returning immediately.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning -1 when x isn't present (treating it like exact search), mixing up which half to keep for floor vs ceil, or off-by-one with mid ± 1.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Present floor and ceil as mirror searches, handle the not-found sentinel cleanly, and connect them to lower_bound / upper_bound and insertion position.

problemStatement:
Given a sorted (non-decreasing) array `arr` and a value `x`, return the **floor** of `x` (the largest element `≤ x`) and the **ceil** of `x` (the smallest element `≥ x`).

If no floor exists (every element is greater than `x`), return a sentinel such as `−1` for the floor. Likewise return `−1` for the ceil if no element is `≥ x`.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶, arr sorted in non-decreasing order
Values fit in a 32-bit integer (use long for mid only if indices are huge — here indices fit)
Return a sentinel (−1) when floor or ceil does not exist
understanding: On a sorted array you want the nearest element that doesn't overshoot (floor) and the nearest that doesn't undershoot (ceil) relative to x. Because the array is ordered, the set of elements ≤ x forms a prefix and the set ≥ x forms a suffix, so each boundary can be found by binary search instead of a scan — keep the best candidate as you converge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return when floor or ceil doesn't exist?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A sentinel like −1 (or report 'none'). Confirm, because returning the wrong sentinel is a common silent bug.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. With duplicates equal to x, floor and ceil both equal x; the ≤/≥ comparisons handle it without special cases.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Binary search requires it. If not sorted, you'd sort first (O(n log n)) or scan linearly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want the values or their indices?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either is easy — record the candidate index instead of the value if positions are needed.

approaches.name: Linear Scan
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this — it makes the definitions concrete and sets up why the sorted order lets us do better.
hints: Walk the array once. Track the largest value seen that is ≤ x (floor) and, separately, the smallest value that is ≥ x (ceil).
Because the array is sorted you could stop early, but a plain scan ignores that and checks everything.
n comparisons per query — fine for small n, wasteful when n is large or there are many queries.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n elements with O(1) work each → O(n). Constant extra space for the two candidates.
approaches.explanation:
The definition-driven baseline simply checks every element.

**The literal method.** Iterate once. Each element ≤ x updates the floor candidate (since the array is non-decreasing, the last such element is the true floor). The first element ≥ x is the ceil. Keep both as you go.

**Why it's correct but slow.** It never uses the sorted structure beyond a possible early exit. For a single small array it's perfectly fine and is the clearest way to state what floor and ceil mean. But with `n` up to 10⁶ or many queries against the same array, paying `O(n)` per query is exactly what binary search removes.
approaches.insight: The scan's cost comes from ignoring order. Sorted data means 'elements ≤ x' is a contiguous prefix — so the floor is just the last index of that prefix, which binary search finds in O(log n).

java.explanation: Sorted order means the last element ≤ x is the floor.
The first element ≥ x is the ceil; lock it once.

python.explanation: Keep overwriting — final value is the largest ≤ x.
Capture the first element that reaches x.

approaches.name: Binary Search for the Boundary (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Stress that you record a candidate and keep searching the better side instead of returning on an exact hit.
hints: The elements ≤ x form a prefix of the sorted array; the floor is the last element of that prefix. Binary-search for that boundary.
When arr[mid] ≤ x, mid is a valid floor candidate — record it and search right (lo = mid + 1) for a possibly larger valid value. Otherwise search left.
Ceil mirrors it: when arr[mid] ≥ x, record it and search left (hi = mid − 1) for a smaller valid value; otherwise search right.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each comparison halves the range, so O(log n) iterations, each O(1) → O(log n) time and O(1) extra space per query.
approaches.explanation:
Both floor and ceil are the same binary search with mirrored comparisons; the key change from textbook binary search is that you don't stop on an exact match — you stash a candidate and keep going toward the best one.

**Floor — largest element ≤ x.** The values `≤ x` occupy a prefix of the array, and the floor is that prefix's last element. Run binary search: at `mid`, if `arr[mid] <= x`, then `mid` qualifies, so record `arr[mid]` as the current best and move right (`lo = mid + 1`) to look for an even larger value that still doesn't exceed `x`. If `arr[mid] > x`, this position overshoots, so move left (`hi = mid − 1`). When the loop ends, the last recorded candidate is the floor; if nothing was ever recorded, return `−1`.

**Ceil — smallest element ≥ x.** Mirror everything. The values `≥ x` form a suffix, and the ceil is its first element. At `mid`, if `arr[mid] >= x`, record it and move left (`hi = mid − 1`) seeking a smaller value still at least `x`. If `arr[mid] < x`, move right (`lo = mid + 1`). The last recorded candidate is the ceil.

**Why equality needs no special case.** If `x` is present, the `<=` in floor and the `>=` in ceil both treat the equal element as a valid candidate, so floor and ceil naturally collapse to `x`. You don't branch on 'found exactly'.

**Overflow-safe mid.** Compute `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2` rather than `(lo + hi) / 2`; for large indices the latter can overflow. It also keeps the off-by-one reasoning clean: the `mid ± 1` updates guarantee the window strictly shrinks, so the loop always terminates.

**Relation to lower_bound / upper_bound.** Ceil is exactly `lower_bound(x)` (first element `≥ x`); the element just before `upper_bound(x)` is the floor. Recognising floor/ceil as these standard boundaries lets you reuse one mental template for insertion position, nearest element, and range counting.
approaches.insight: Plain binary search answers 'is x here?'. Floor/ceil answer 'what's the nearest element on this side?' — same halving, but you carry a candidate and lean toward x from one direction. That candidate-carrying tweak is the whole pattern behind lower_bound, upper_bound, and 'search for a boundary' problems generally.

pitfalls: Returning -1 when x isn't present — that's exact-match behaviour, not floor/ceil.
Swapping the kept half between floor and ceil and getting the opposite answer.
Using (lo + hi) / 2 and overflowing on large indices.
Forgetting to initialise the candidate to the sentinel, so a missing floor/ceil reads stale data.

edgeCases.behavior: Floor and ceil both equal x; the ≤/≥ comparisons collapse them correctly.
Loop never runs → both return the sentinel -1.

commonMistakes: Returning -1 for a missing exact match instead of the nearest floor/ceil.
Keeping the wrong half — searching left for floor or right for ceil.
Integer overflow from (lo + hi) / 2 on large indices.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating it like exact search
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Floor/ceil must return the nearest element on the correct side even when x is absent. Returning -1 just because arr[mid] never equals x defeats the purpose.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Searching the wrong half
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For floor you must move right after a hit (to find a larger valid value); for ceil you move left. Swapping them returns the opposite boundary.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// floor, but moving left after a valid candidate
if (arr[mid] <= x) { ans = arr[mid]; hi = mid - 1; } // wrong direction
commonMistakesDetailed.good: if (arr[mid] <= x) { ans = arr[mid]; lo = mid + 1; }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow in the midpoint
commonMistakesDetailed.why: (lo + hi) can overflow a 32-bit int for large indices, producing a negative mid and out-of-bounds access. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

patternNote: Binary search for a boundary (lower_bound / upper_bound). Recognise it whenever you need the nearest element on one side of x in sorted data: record the candidate, keep narrowing toward x, return the sentinel when none exists. Floor and ceil are the canonical mirror pair.
